Classic

Draft an all-time lineup from every era. Win the pennant, or win it all.

How to play

About

Stacked Deck 1.0
Not affiliated with Major League Baseball, the MLB Players Association or any team.

Info

GM Simulator

  • Build a dynasty. Take over one team in a full league and run it season after season: the lineup, the pitching staff, trades, the draft, contracts and free agency.
  • Start from any season since 1980 with real rosters, a fantasy draft of real players, or a league of random players. Real leagues follow history: expansions, division changes, team moves and each era's DH rule and playoff format.
  • Real players are rated from their real stats. Real Player Determinism sets how closely they follow their actual careers each spring, and Real Retirements and Real Injuries do the same for when they retire and the time they miss. Real drafts are used through 2026; later draft classes are generated.
  • Play a day at a time or sim ahead: 7 days, 30 days, to the All-Star break, the trade deadline, the end of the regular season or through the playoffs. Watch any of your games live with a running box score. Stop for big moments pauses a sim when something big happens to your team.
  • Your lineup and pitching staff stay as you set them until you change them, and you can switch back to auto anytime. Injured players are covered from the bench until they return.
  • Pitchers tire as their pitch count climbs. Starters need 4 days of rest. Relievers need rest after long outings and never pitch 3 days in a row. Name a closer and up to 2 setup men; the rest of the bullpen is used by the score.
  • Each team has a 40-man roster plus a farm system of up to 15 prospects. Keep at least 12 position players and 10 pitchers: the game asks you to fill any gap before it sims.
  • Trade players and draft picks, answer offers from other teams (decline, counter or accept, with undo until the next day), or put players on the trading block. Players you just traded for, signed or drafted can't be traded right away. Trading closes at the deadline and reopens at the draft.
  • Contracts: 3 years at the minimum salary, then 3 arbitration years, then free agency. Re-sign or non-tender players in the offseason and stay within your owner's budget, which is smaller on harder difficulty. You can turn the budget off.
  • The offseason runs awards and the Hall of Fame, retirements, the draft, re-signing, free agency, then spring training.
  • Each league has its own settings: games per season, playoff format, DH rule, draft order and rounds, injuries and difficulty.
  • Leagues save on this device as you play. Clearing this site's browser data deletes them.

Pack mode

  • Stack the deck. Win it all. Rip packs of legends, build the strongest roster you can, and see if it wins the pennant or wins it all.
  • Every pack shows its decade on the wrapper before you rip it, and the cards inside are on that decade's card stock.
  • Rip a pack to get 3 cards from one decade. Each decade holds about 50 to 110 players fans know: Hall of Famers, All-Stars, award winners and milestone leaders, with limits by position. Relievers: 10 per decade from the 1980s on (8 in the 1970s, 5 in the 1960s, 3 in the 1950s). Catchers in the 1910s, 1920s and 1940s are Hall of Fame caliber only. Fill 11 spots: C, 1B, 2B, 3B, SS, LF, CF, RF, DH, SP and RP.
  • Packs from the 1980s to the 2020s come up 1.5 times as often as packs from the 1920s, 1930s, 1950s and 1960s. 1970s packs come up 1.25 times as often, and 1910s and 1940s packs 0.8 times as often. Legends (the top 30% of each decade by fame) are a little rarer than other cards.
  • You get 10 packs to fill 11 spots. Take as many cards from a pack as fit your open spots, or none: there is no minimum. Cards you leave are gone. The counter at the top shows how many packs you have left.
  • Every pack before the last one has at least one card that fits an open spot. The next-to-last pack has at least two when you have two or more spots open.
  • The last pack is a gamble. With 1 open spot it can fill it 95% of the time, with 2 open spots it can fill both 70% of the time, and with 3 open spots it can fill all three 30% of the time. Any spot left empty is a forfeit. Fill your roster in the first 9 packs (11 spots, so take a second card from at least 2 packs) and you never have to gamble.
  • Every spot comes up about equally often: about 1 card in 8 can play any given spot, so a 10-pack draft deals about 4 cards for each spot. Packs also lean toward the spots you still need: a card that fits one of your open spots (other than DH) is 1.5 times as likely as one that doesn't. Most cards are hitters because every hitter can also play DH. Relievers start in the 1950s, so later packs carry more of them.
  • Negro Leagues stars (1920s to 1940s) and Japanese stars from NPB (1960s to 1990s) appear in their decades. Their stats are scaled to 162 games and rated on the same scale as major leaguers. NPB cards show n/a for WAR because none is on record, so their rating comes from their stats against major leaguers of the same decade.
  • Draft advice fills each draft button left to right. A full green button means a better player for that spot is unlikely to turn up in your remaining packs: take him now. A short red button means a better one is likely later. In between (yellow) could go either way. The meter is the chance that no better player turns up, so it grows with every pack you rip: a short red button early can turn green later. It is an estimate from the pack odds and does not count your pace: the note under the buttons tells you when you need extra cards. It does not show on the last pack. The Advice button at the top turns it on or off.
  • Card types: Common is a decade average. All-Star averages his top 3 All-Star seasons in the decade. MVP and Cy Young cards are award seasons. Reliever of the Year cards are award seasons. Hall of Fame cards are the player's best season in any decade.
  • Each card is rated 0 to 100 against every card at that spot from all decades, by WAR per 162 games: oWAR plus dWAR in the field, oWAR at DH, and pitching WAR for starters and relievers. A 1920s card and a 2010s card with the same WAR get the same rating. The buttons under a card are the spots he can play, with his rating at each one; a player can rate differently at two spots because each spot has its own pool. Your record comes from the combined rating of the 11 players.

Lotto spin

Players show after you lock it in.

How it works

  • Stack the deck. Win it all. Draft an all-time lineup from every era. The stronger the lineup, the more wins: win the pennant, or win it all.
  • Fill 11 spots: C, 1B, 2B, 3B, SS, LF, CF, RF, DH, SP and RP. Any hitter can play DH.
  • Each round, spin a team and a decade. The roster appears below the spin. Sort it by any stat, then draft a player into an open position on the field.
  • You get 2 team respins (the decade stays locked), 2 decade respins (the team stays locked) and 1 career year boost for the whole draft. The boost shows career years for the current spin only, and a respin cancels it.
  • A team change always stays in the same decade. A decade change always stays with the same franchise, including its earlier and later homes: MON and WSN, PHA, KCA and OAK, WSH and MIN, BSN, MLN and ATL, BRO and LAD, NYG and SFG, SLB and BAL.
  • Lotto spin, once per game: it locks either the team or the decade at random. You scroll the other one and pick it yourself, and the players show once you lock it in. Only teams with a player who fits an open spot are listed. Use it in place of a spin, or to replace the spin you just got.
  • Every card uses the same basis: the average of a player's best 3 seasons with that team in that decade (all of his seasons if he had fewer than 3), per 162 team games. Best means highest sWAR. The boost swaps in his single best season with that team in that decade.
  • The roster only lists players who fit a spot you still have open. Every hitter can play DH, so once DH is filled, a hitter drops off the list when his field positions are filled too.
  • When only RP is left, spins land on teams with a 20-save reliever.
  • The 1969 expansion teams (KCR, SEP, SDP and MON) are left out of the 1960s because each played only one season that decade. Those franchises start in the 1970s.
  • Teams show by franchise code, such as NYY and NYM, CHC and CHW, PHI and PHA, STL and SLB, BOS and BSN, LAD and LAA. The small label above the code names the city.
  • sWAR (Stacked WAR) is a player's score from the stats on his card. Each stat is compared with the median player at his main position across every decade, and his sWAR is the same at any spot he can play, DH included, so era luck is part of the game: a 1910s ace has a tiny ERA, a 2000s slugger has big home run totals. Roughly, each of these adds 1 point of sWAR: 15 to 20 home runs, 60 runs, 130 RBI, 50 steals, .050 of OBP, .090 of batting average, or 1.3 dWAR. For starters: 0.60 lower ERA, 60 more innings, 100 more strikeouts, or 23 wins (each loss costs a little more than a win adds). For closers: 1.30 lower ERA, 100 more innings, 150 more strikeouts, or 50 saves. sWAR is the default sort.
  • Each player shows the stats you would find on the back of his baseball card. Hitters: AVG, OBP, HR, R, RBI, SB and dWAR (defensive WAR). Pitchers: W-L, ERA, IP and SO, plus SV for relievers. Sort by any of them from the menu.
  • Your record comes from the stats on your 11 cards, added up through sWAR, at about 7 wins per point. The scale is set on a player who takes the best available player on every spin and uses one team respin and one decade respin (on spins where the best player available is under +2.5 sWAR), with no boost and no lotto spin. He goes 81-81 half the time, and 2% of his drafts go 162-0. Your second team and decade respins, the boost and the lotto spin are how you beat those odds. The results screen shows your lineup as a box score: each player, your team totals, and the stat lines of a typical 81-81 team and a typical 162-0 team.

Stats: Lahman Baseball Database and Baseball-Reference WAR. Seasons 1910 to 2025, excluding 2020. AL and NL only.
